<thoughtml version="1.0">
  <task>Investigate why a test loaf collapsed.</task>
  <subject>Bakery test loaf failure</subject>
  <question>What most likely caused the loaf to collapse?</question>

  <known_facts>
    <fact id="F1">The yeast was fresh.</fact>
    <fact id="F2">The oven reached its target temperature.</fact>
    <fact id="F3">The dough received twice the intended amount of water.</fact>
    <fact id="F4">Proofing time was slightly short.</fact>
    <fact id="F5">The baker believes excessive hydration caused the collapse.</fact>
  </known_facts>

  <hypotheses>
    <hypothesis id="H1" label="Excessive hydration caused structural failure" stance="primary">
      <support>
        <point>Doubling the intended water level would substantially weaken dough structure.</point>
        <point>Overly wet dough can fail to retain shape and gas, increasing collapse risk.</point>
        <point>This is the largest reported deviation from the intended process.</point>
      </support>
      <counterpoints>
        <point>No direct measurement of gluten development or dough strength is provided.</point>
      </counterpoints>
    </hypothesis>

    <hypothesis id="H2" label="Slightly short proofing contributed to the collapse" stance="secondary">
      <support>
        <point>Proofing affects gas retention and final loaf structure.</point>
        <point>A process deviation in proofing was present.</point>
      </support>
      <counterpoints>
        <point>The proofing issue was described as only slight.</point>
        <point>Short proofing more often limits expansion than explains a full collapse by itself.</point>
        <point>This deviation appears less severe than doubling the water.</point>
      </counterpoints>
    </hypothesis>

    <hypothesis id="H3" label="Yeast failure caused the collapse" stance="weak">
      <support>
        <point>Yeast problems can affect loaf performance.</point>
      </support>
      <counterpoints>
        <point>The yeast was fresh, reducing the likelihood of yeast failure.</point>
      </counterpoints>
    </hypothesis>

    <hypothesis id="H4" label="Oven temperature failure caused the collapse" stance="weak">
      <support>
        <point>Incorrect oven temperature can damage loaf structure.</point>
      </support>
      <counterpoints>
        <point>The oven reached its target temperature, so this explanation is not supported by the reported facts.</point>
      </counterpoints>
    </hypothesis>
  </hypotheses>

  <evidence_assessment>
    <most_supportive_evidence>
      <item>The dough received twice the intended amount of water.</item>
      <item>Fresh yeast and correct oven temperature remove two common alternative explanations.</item>
    </most_supportive_evidence>
    <competing_evidence>
      <item>Slightly short proofing could have contributed to poor structure or reduced readiness.</item>
    </competing_evidence>
    <weighing>
      <item>Hydration error is the strongest causal factor because it is severe and directly affects dough strength.</item>
      <item>Short proofing is better interpreted as a secondary contributor than the main cause.</item>
    </weighing>
  </evidence_assessment>

  <conclusion status="present">
    The loaf most likely collapsed because the dough was excessively hydrated after receiving twice the intended amount of water. Slightly short proofing may have contributed, but the available evidence indicates it was a secondary factor rather than the primary cause. Fresh yeast and correct oven temperature make yeast failure and oven underperformance unlikely explanations.
  </conclusion>

  <confidence level="high">
    The conclusion is well supported by the reported process deviations, with excessive hydration standing out as the dominant cause.
  </confidence>
</thoughtml>
